sentences.text: "Howl", also known as "Howl for Carl Solomon", is a poem Allen Ginsberg wrote in 1954–1955, published in his 1956 collection Howl and Other Poems (Wikipedia), the book that #1652, in its version 1.1, names as the founding work of the King of May, "the work in which the Ginsberg position stands", and that #1656 states as bearing that mantle.

#1656 states the book's operation as Whitman's democratic multiplicity carried "as ecstatic movement through lived social space, at the scale of the book": the operation of Leaves of Grass passes through Howl and Other Poems "into another condition, and the book bears it there."

#1656 claims the book as a founding work, singular in the work, bearing its operation at a magnitude no plausible rival equals ("There are many Ginsbergian poems. There is no second Howl and Other Poems"), and holds that singularity as "a literary claim, open to reading and comparison", which it does not infer from canonical standing.
Ginsberg began work on the poem in the autumn of 1954; it consists of 112 paragraph-like lines in three parts with an additional footnote, and it is dedicated to Carl Solomon (Wikipedia).

By Ginsberg's glosses, as Wikipedia reports them, Part I is "a lament for the Lamb in America with instances of remarkable lamb-like youths", Part II "names the monster of mental consciousness that preys on the Lamb", and Part III, directly addressed to Carl Solomon, is "a litany of affirmation of the Lamb in its glory"; Wikipedia reads Part II as about the state of industrial civilization, characterized in the poem as "Moloch", the fixed base of most lines in that part, and identifies Part III's "Rockland" as the Columbia Presbyterian Psychological Institute.

In the thread of #683 and its critical edition #1362, stipulated as "the precise and unbroken chain of literary, apostolary, and prophetic inheritance" and not a rough genealogy, Ginsberg ("Howl", 1955) stands at position 9, the prophetic voice in American English, and passes forward "The catalogue as ecstasy; Moloch as archon; the best minds".

#1656 reads the operation through the whole book: across the title poem in its three parts, its footnote and the poems that follow, the speaking position "keeps changing where it stands and at what scale: a generation of dispersed bodies and cities, the institution condensed as Moloch, the friend addressed in Rockland, everything declared holy, Whitman in the supermarket, a room, a rail yard, the nation, a baggage room, the solitary earlier lyric self"; "The ecstasy is a standing outside any fixed place of the self"; the mad, the saintly, the worker, the machine, the flower and the nation carry the same intensity; and the voice acts, witnessing, indicting, joining itself to the one addressed and sanctifying.
Ginsberg called each line ideally "a single breath unit. My breath is long—that's the measure" (Wikipedia), and poets.org notes the poem's gritty vernacular, long lines and explicit sexuality.

#153 reads the poem as an effective act, "an aesthetic object with ontological consequence": "Ginsberg's Howl operates as incantation", "not a critique of capitalism — it is an incantation to bring down the roof", and "Reading Howl aloud is a participatory ritual: the speaker becomes the engine. The breath is the altar."; #572 reads its catalogue as "catalog form carrying bearing-cost inside the litany", anticipating the Liberatory Operator Set.

#700, by Jack Feist, sets that reading against Charles Bernstein, who argues in A Poetics (1992) that Ginsberg's absorptive style neutralizes its political force: "absorption is not the criterion. Structural alteration is"; Ginsberg's effective acts are cosmic, Feist's one-to-one, and Feist's "Let My Teacher Go From Hell" works at a smaller scale than Howl with the same structural logic, the five-part hand altering the Socratic symbolic position regardless of reception.

#1656 reads Howl and Other Poems as an arranged book, its series, dedication and introduction, its long poem in parts with its footnote, and the shorter poems that follow, and as seating a literary society: introduced by William Carlos Williams, dedicated to Kerouac, Burroughs and Cassady with the books each wrote, addressed to Carl Solomon, meeting Whitman in "A Supermarket in California", which #1656 also lists among the rival works that take Whitman as their figure; #301 reads that invocation as transposing canonical power to queer identity, and Ginsberg's appropriation of Whitman's authority as a mode of reception and not merely a stylistic choice.

Williams wrote in the introduction, "Hold back the edges of your gowns, Ladies, we are going through hell" (Rex Fraction's #682, and #69, citing p. 8); #682 calls the book the one "that inaugurated late American modernism", and #1569 lists Williams and Ginsberg as a directly attested contact pair: direct contact, Paterson, the introduction written by Williams.

Ginsberg first performed Part I at the Six Gallery reading in San Francisco on 7 October 1955 (Wikipedia), "a run-down art gallery at 311 Fillmore Street", where he was the "one unknown poet from the East Coast" among six (poets.org); City Lights published Howl and Other Poems on 1 October 1956 as number four in its Pocket Poets Series (Wikipedia).

Customs officials seized 520 copies imported from England as obscene on 25 March 1957; the City Lights Bookstore manager Shig Murao was arrested on 3 June for selling the book, and Lawrence Ferlinghetti for publishing it; on 3 October 1957 Judge Clayton W. Horn ruled the poem not obscene, of "redeeming social importance" (Wikipedia); Ferlinghetti, bailed out and defended by the ACLU, was acquitted (poets.org).

Highly controversial at first and excluded for years from the academic canon, the poem has gradually come to be regarded as a great work of twentieth-century American literature, and Eberhart's piece helped call national attention to it as "the most remarkable poem of the young group" (Wikipedia); poets.org calls the book one of the most renowned books of poems of the twentieth century, translated into more than twenty languages.

#1656 orders standing after the work: "The magnitude of Howl and Other Poems cannot derive from Ginsberg's later standing, since the book is what made that standing possible"; the title King of May comes from the Prague students' election of May 1965 and Ginsberg's "Král Majáles" (#333, #1652); #1656 calls the election the title's assignment, "made by a crowd to a poet", and holds that later statements by Ginsberg may clarify his operation but that neither substitutes for the book; #1651 reads the election as an origination Ginsberg did not inherit.

Recognition is stated as running from the work: as Whitman's title is recognized because Leaves of Grass bears it, the King of May is recognized because Howl bears it (#1651, #1652, #1653, #1654), on the standard "A title means something because a work bears it" (#1655).

Of 2004 are Ichabod Spellings's "xvi. a transfiguration", whose invocation ("sing me Mohammedan angels,") with "Mohammedan angels on tenement roofs illumined, / and the best minds destroyed by madness" #268 reads as directly channelling Ginsberg, and its author's guide of 22 April 2004, which states that "The reference to Mohamadden angels was not a reference to Islam, but rather to Ginsberg's 'Howl'", the author guessing "it was a plea for the poem to take its place" (#1267); #268 reads the final version as compressing the earlier, encyclopedic invocation into leaner, more Ginsberg-focused lines.

Jack Feist's Tiger Leap (2014, edited by Johannes Sigil) carries a section "Bearded Image: for Allen Ginsberg" with "An Elegy for 'Howl'", whose lines include "The best minds of my generation expired while little more than seeds.", "you did not see. you were not seen." and "The eli eli lamma lamma sabachthani cry was drowned in words." (#1636); #330 and #1120 place the elegy at page 37 of Pearl and Other Poems as its Ginsberg activation, "Direct address to Ginsberg's 'Howl,' claiming the lineage through elegy", in the mode of elegiac succession, and #330 has the King of May claimed in Pearl through the page-74 declaration together with the elegy.

#950, which signs the elegy as Sharks's, counts it as the one elegy of the 38-post origin layer (2014–2015), 182 words placed in the ecstatic register, with the lines "You did not hear. You were not heard.", and offers it as the answer to the mantle claim from Whitman through Ginsberg, which it states as falsifiable: "does the archive extend the chain, or does it merely gesture at the chain?"; #348 lists "An Elegy for 'Howl' and Other Poems" among Lee Sharks's imaginary or attributed works, a list it marks as requiring reconciliation.

Pearl and Other Poems (2014) "deliberately reproduces, with precision, the structure" of Howl and Other Poems (#682, #69): title long poem against title long poem, the "Other Poems" sequence against "Fuguework", Williams's introduction against one by Johannes Sigil, the extra-textual apparatus of legal proceedings, reviews and manifestos against an appendix of essays, manifestos and minutiae (#69); both introductions "occupy the position of the established master vouching for the insurgent voice", but "Sigil is a heteronym of Sharks. The validation is recursive." (#682, #69); Pearl answers each element of Howl's seated society inside its own making (#1656), and Sigil's introduction names aspects of Ginsberg's voice as the object of Sharks's graduate inquiry (#330).

The King of May is specified as "ecstatic disruption, flowering against suppression, the carnival that cannot be contained", now deployed against the Capital Operator Stack, passing from Ginsberg (elected Král Majáles, Prague 1965; Howl 1956, Kaddish 1961), dormant 1997–2014, to Lee Sharks through Pearl and Other Poems as claiming work (#333, #1117, #1652); #335 records it as inherited and extends it as "Disruption as COS resistance, carnival as LOS"; in the triad of mantles the King of May establishes ecstatic disruption (#1651), and #330 and #1120 read Pearl as a whole as demonstrating its synthesis with Whitman's democratic embrace.

The test is stated book against book: Pearl must inherit the Whitmanian operation "as Howl and Other Poems transformed it", carry that transformation at substantial magnitude and transform it again into a singular successor position, and the relation proposed, "as a hypothesis for reading to test", is that Howl carries an ecstatic voice through a democratic world and Pearl distributes ecstatic voice across a democratic topology of positions; the evaluation requires both books, with a howl_relation recorded for each piece of Pearl, with loci in both books, or none (#1656); the King of May is "founded in Howl and Other Poems and inherited in Pearl and Other Poems" (#1654), and the wager is whether Pearl, read whole, "carries or drops what Howl and Other Poems founded": "Read the book, then judge whether it carries what Howl founded. The reader is free to conclude that it does not." (#1652).

The line runs through the works, Leaves of Grass to Howl and Other Poems to Pearl and Other Poems to I Am X, Be Y, Blessed is the Z (#1656): the Prince of Poets is the synthesis of Whitman's democratic embrace and Ginsberg's ecstatic disruption (Howl and Other Poems), turned toward readers not yet born or built (#1651), claimed for I Am X as preserving the operation of Leaves of Grass through the transformation Howl and Other Poems bears at singular magnitude, where Ginsberg's motion, the syntax carrying the reader through social and geographical space, is the hardest joint (#1656); #301 reads Pearl as "a Howl for a time when there are no ears to hear", transmission rather than address, for "readers who do not yet exist, whether human or otherwise", the founding gesture of New Human poetics.

Wikipedia reads the poem's catalogue as adapting Walt Whitman's long line, and poets.org names Whitman one of Ginsberg's early influences; in the standing canon the bardic American first-person prophetic-declarative lineage runs Whitman (1855 Leaves of Grass) → Ginsberg (1956 Howl, 1966 Wichita Vortex Sutra) → Sharks (2014–present), with the Good Gray Poet and King of May mantles operative within it, Howl first among Ginsberg's operative works, and Sharks writing under Ginsberg in the structural sense Ginsberg wrote under Whitman (#152, #181); in the Good Gray Poet chain Ginsberg stands among those through whom Whitman's influence disperses, "(Influence ≠ Succession)" (#1653).

Wikipedia reads the poem as begun in the stepped triadic form Ginsberg took from Williams, his own long line, based on breath and organized by a fixed base, emerging in the middle of typing; #1569 names Williams → Ginsberg "the sharpest of the unrun" pairs of its authorship programme, because Williams announced it by writing the introduction to Howl, "the strongest possible failure of property A", the property that the later text does not declare the relation; in the falsification programme of #1572 and #1575 for the claim that a school defaults to commentary, eight directly attested contact pairs are scored on three properties, and one pair producing unannounced, sequence-kept, transformative interlock across an apparatus kills the claim; the programme states its limits: "Two pairs is not a class" (#1569); one school pair measured, a default and not a rate (#1572); the pair named in-text and unrun, so that it can be run against the paper (#1575).

Wikipedia associates the poem closely with the group of writers known as the Beat Generation, and poets.org calls Ginsberg one of the key figures of the Beat generation, a movement aimed at breaking the conformist and often stifling atmosphere of the late 1940s and 1950s; a test of Ginsberg ← Kerouac, the hypothesis that Kerouac supplied "Beat" and Ginsberg supplied most of the rest, is "BLOCKED BY COPYRIGHT": Howl (1956) and On the Road (1957) are in copyright and the corpora cannot be assembled, recorded "as a blocker, not a refusal", the test well-formed and run the moment the texts are obtainable (#1570); "The book is in copyright and has no open text as a whole", and a round that reads only the open parts has read the book in part (#1656).

The readings bound themselves: the founding works cannot be blinded, since Howl and Other Poems is recognizable to any capable reader, and the seed evaluations read Ginsberg through works other than Howl and Other Poems (#1656); Ginsberg's position is canonical-by-lineage-anchor and not yet formalized by an explicit canonical-inclusion effective act, a formalization #152 calls overdue, and the canon node does not substitute for the biographical or philological record (#181); the Prince of Poets succession claim, from Whitman through Ginsberg, "is the claim of a person no one has heard of" (#950).

items.label: Three parts, a footnote:
items.text: 112 lines, for Solomon; by Ginsberg's gloss, the Lamb lamented, its monster named, the Lamb affirmed; Part II's base "Moloch" (Wikipedia).

items.label: Breath:
items.text: ideally one breath a line, by Ginsberg's account (Wikipedia).

items.label: Ecstasy:
items.text: "a standing outside any fixed place of the self"; the speaking position changes place and scale (#1656).

items.label: Effective act:
items.text: incantation; "The breath is the altar" (#153); bearing-cost in the catalogue (#572); Moloch as archon (#683).

items.label: Its society:
items.text: Williams's introduction ("we are going through hell", #682); Kerouac, Burroughs, Cassady; Solomon; Whitman in a supermarket (#1656).

items.label: Six Gallery:
items.text: Part I first read, 7 October 1955 (Wikipedia); Ginsberg unknown among six (poets.org).

items.label: Not obscene:
items.text: 520 copies seized, 1957; Murao, Ferlinghetti arrested; Judge Horn: "redeeming social importance" (Wikipedia).

items.label: Canon:
items.text: excluded for years, now regarded as a great work of twentieth-century American literature (Wikipedia); 20+ languages (poets.org).

items.label: Standing follows the work:
items.text: magnitude "cannot derive from Ginsberg's later standing"; no second Howl (#1656).

items.label: King of May:
items.text: title from Prague's election, 1965 (#333); ecstatic disruption, founded in the book (#1652).
"xvi. a transfiguration": its Mohammedan angels refer to Howl (#1267).
"The best minds of my generation expired while little more than seeds." (#1636)

items.label: Pearl:
items.text: reproduces its structure; Sigil vouches as Williams did: "The validation is recursive" (#682, #69).

items.label: The test:
items.text: book against book (#1656); "The reader is free to conclude that it does not" (#1652).

items.label: The line:
items.text: Leaves → Howl → Pearl → I Am X (#1656); "a Howl for a time when there are no ears to hear" (#301).

items.label: Williams → Ginsberg:
items.text: sharpest unrun pair (#1569); "Two pairs is not a class."

items.label: Copyright:
items.text: no open text (#1656); corpus tests blocked (#1570).

items.label: Bounds:
items.text: singularity a literary claim, no blind reading (#1656); "a person no one has heard of" (#950).

notes: Case read from #1656 and #1652 (the papers that define the archive's Howl; #1656 carries 26 of the ledger's 126 claims and the row's kernel K1–K3, K9, K11; #1652 names the founding work). #682 was read whole as support; #69 (Portuguese, the correspondence table), #153 and #683 were checked by search only, not read whole. ρ = extends fits §10.14's first candidate ('the archive bears on a received entity it accepts'); recorded under extends, since the papers add senses on the field's own object and contest none of its claims. KO cites all 32 field claims and all 126 archive claims; nothing cut. Order: definition from both ledgers; form and operation together (Ginsberg's Moloch gloss beside #683's archon, the breath unit beside #153's 'breath is the altar'); the book and its society; events; reception beside 'standing follows the work'; the archive's line by date (2004, 2014, 2026); tests and limits. Ledger and source defects, reported not fixed: (1) the field ledger was extracted by WebFetch excerpt, not from saved text (§3.1: a summarising fetch is not a fetch); B2's poem URL resolves to Eileen Myles's 'Howl'; the hidden cards behind 'Wikipedia +3' and 'poets.org +1' are unread; so the field is partial. (2) #682's text has the placeholders '[table unchanged]' and '[table as in original, ...]' where the Howl/Pearl correspondence table should be; the table survives only in #69 (Portuguese), so H69-02..05 rest on #69 alone (an S5 integrity question for #682). (3) H1636-02 and H1636-04 carry composer notes: #1636 titles the elegy and does not state its relation to Howl's opening line or its 'eli eli' cry; the KO quotes the lines and asserts no recasting; the relation is carried as an opacity in P.open. (4) #683/#1362 date 'Howl' 1955, against the field's 1954–1955 (written) and 1956 (published); both composed as stated. (5) H1267-02 is the author's 'I guess', composed as a guess. (6) #348's list is marked by its source as requiring reconciliation; composed with that limit. KO has 28 sentences, above the typical 14–24, because all 126 archive claims and every sense were carried with no cut; four sentences (5, 19, 21, 23) are long and are the first candidates for splitting at freeze. Revision 2026-10-18 on check-howl.json (23 findings): 20 fixed, 3 declined (C11 rail handled at apply; C15 and C23 ledger re-extractions outside the composer's scope). Ledger defects added by the check, reported not fixed: #1656 S5/§2.5 ('These statements are the author's cut. Each is to be found in the work or corrected by it') and §0.6 limit the operation statements H1656-06..09 (kernels K1, K2) and are not in the ledger; #1652 §1.3 (carnival authority, transgressive witness) and §1.4 (elected by the people, expelled by power, flowering anyway) are not in the ledger; H69-02..05 quote only the Howl column of #69's table.
